geology-hills: Hills are modest rises of ground that never quite reach mountain status — usually under a few hundred metres of relief, with rounded crests that erosion softens over time. They form from leftover ridges, glacial deposits, faulted blocks, or volcanic mounds, and their gentle slopes make them natural homes for farms and towns. A hill is simply a mountain in its youth, or a mountain that time has worn down.
geology-buttes-and-mesas: Mesas and buttes are flat-topped islands of rock left standing while the land around them erodes. A mesa is the wide table (Spanish for 'table'), and a butte is its slimmer, taller remnant once the edges retreat. Both wear a hard caprock — often basalt or sandstone — that protects the softer layers beneath. The American Southwest is full of them, monuments to millions of years of wind and water stripping the landscape.
geology-plateaus-types: Plateaus are large, flat, high-elevation surfaces that come in three flavours: volcanic plateaus built from stacked lava flows, like the Columbia Plateau; continental plateaus raised as whole blocks, like the Tibetan; and dissected plateaus that erosion has carved into canyons and mesas, like the Colorado. All three share the same surprise — flat land sitting thousands of metres up, often topped with marine fossils that prove the sea once covered them.
geology-tibetan-plateau: The Tibetan Plateau is the highest and largest plateau on Earth, averaging 4,500 metres above sea level and spanning about 2.5 million square kilometres. It formed when the Indian plate collided with Asia roughly 50 million years ago, crumpling the crust into the Himalayas and doubling the plateau's thickness. Its thin air and cold climate drive the monsoon system: heating the plateau pumps moisture across Asia, feeding rivers that a third of humanity drinks from.
geology-basins: Sedimentary basins are broad, sinking regions of the crust that trap sediment over tens of millions of years. Rivers, wind, and seas pour material into them, and each layer buries the one before, compressing sand into sandstone and mud into shale. Because they collect thick organic-rich sediment, basins are where most of the world's oil, gas, coal, and groundwater hide — and where geologists read Earth's history page by page.
geology-structural-basins: Structural basins are bowl-shaped downwarps in the crust, formed when rock layers sag under weight, stretch, or the pull of faulting. Unlike sedimentary basins, which simply collect material, structural basins bend the rock itself into a concave dish. The Michigan Basin, a giant buried bowl, holds more than 4,000 metres of Paleozoic rock in its centre. The youngest layers sit in the middle, and the oldest ring the edges — the opposite of a dome.
geology-horsts-and-grabens: Horsts and grabens are paired blocks of crust produced by extension: when the land stretches, faults crack it into slices, and alternating blocks drop down (grabens, from the German for 'ditch') while neighbours rise (horsts, meaning 'heap'). The result is a landscape of parallel valleys and ridges, like Nevada's Basin and Range province. Death Valley is a famous graben — its floor is still sinking while the mountains beside it climb.
geology-escarpments: An escarpment is a long cliff or steep slope separating two levels of gently sloping land. Many are fault scarps, the raw face of a fault that slipped; others are erosion fronts where a resistant caprock holds up an edge while softer rock crumbles away. The Niagara Escarpment, a 700-kilometre arc across Ontario, drops over 300 metres in places. Escarpments often mark the edges of ancient uplifted plains or the rims of continental rifts.
geology-drainage-basins: A drainage basin is the entire area of land that funnels rain and snowmelt into a single river system. Every raindrop that falls inside it eventually flows toward the same outlet — a sea, lake, or bigger river. Ridges called divides mark the boundaries between basins. The Amazon's basin covers about 7 million square kilometres, more than any other, and its network carries roughly a fifth of all river water on the planet.
geology-valleys-and-basins-life: Valleys and basins gather what slopes shed: water, soil, and nutrients, making them some of the most fertile places on Earth. Rivers lay down rich floodplains, lakes collect fine sediment, and protected lowlands trap warm air, extending growing seasons. That combination explains why ancient civilizations from the Nile to the Indus chose basins for their cradles — and why today, over half of humanity lives in lowland valleys and coastal basins.
geology-basin-and-range: The Basin and Range province is a vast stretch of western North America where the crust has been pulled apart for about 17 million years. Extension cracked the land into roughly 400 alternating fault blocks — narrow mountain ranges separated by flat sediment-filled basins. As the crust thins and stretches, the ranges keep rising and the basins keep filling. From Nevada into Mexico, the province is Earth's classic textbook example of an extensional landscape.
geology-dome-mountains: Dome mountains form when a blob of magma pushes up from below, swelling the overlying rock into a great rounded arch without breaking it. The Black Hills of South Dakota and the Henry Mountains of Utah are classic examples — the magma later cooled into granite cores that erosion has since exposed. Because the dome's centre is highest, streams radiate outward from it like spokes, carving valleys as they drain.
geology-cuestas: A cuesta is a ridge with an asymmetric profile: a long, gentle slope that follows the dip of the rock layers on one side, and a steep scarp on the other. It forms where a tilted, resistant layer of sandstone or limestone stands proud while weaker beds erode away. The Catskills' escarpment and England's Cotswolds are cuestas. In cross-section they look like a staircase, each step a different resistant bed tilted in the same direction.
geology-hogbacks: A hogback is a narrow, sharp-crested ridge formed when steeply tilted, resistant rock layers stand nearly on edge. Unlike a cuesta's gentle backslope, a hogback shows two steep, symmetrical sides — the beds tilt so steeply that both slopes look alike. They typically form at the eroded limbs of large folds, where softer rock stripped away and left the hard sandstone or limestone spine. Colorado's hogbacks frame the Front Range foothills.
geology-pediments: Pediments are broad, gently sloping bedrock surfaces that skirt the bases of desert mountain ranges, planed smooth by running water and sheetwash. In the American Southwest, they look like flat aprons of gravel sloping away from steep fronts. Over millions of years, erosion strips the range back while the pediment widens, burying the old mountain roots under thin sediment. Pediments show how mountains in dry climates are slowly lowered and consumed.
geology-inselbergs: Inselbergs are isolated rock towers or domes that rise abruptly from flat plains — the German word means 'island mountain'. Uluru in Australia and Sugarloaf Mountain in Brazil are the most famous. They form when erosion strips the softer rock around a particularly resistant mass, often granite, leaving it stranded like an island in the sediment sea. Because they weather slowly, inselbergs can survive for hundreds of millions of years.
geology-playa-basins: Playa basins are flat, dry lake beds found in desert interiors, where water collects after storms and then evaporates completely. Each flood brings in fine silt and dissolved salts; when the water disappears, the salts crystallize into crusts — sometimes dazzling white expanses like Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah. Playas mark the lowest point of an enclosed basin, and their perfectly flat surfaces make them natural speed-testing grounds for land-speed records.
geology-structural-plains: Structural plains are flat regions whose surface follows nearly horizontal rock layers — the landscape mirrors the undisturbed beds beneath. Unlike erosion-carved plains, these surfaces are essentially the original top of the sediment pile, slightly tilted or warped. The Russian Plain and parts of the American Midwest are structural plains. Their flatness and uniform soils make them ideal farmland, and their layered bedrock often hides coal or oil.
geology-basin-hydrology: Water in basins follows gravity's simplest path: rain falls on the surrounding slopes, drains into the low centre, and either seeps into groundwater, evaporates, or escapes through a single outlet. Closed basins with no outlet concentrate salts and become saline lakes or playas; open basins feed rivers to the sea. Groundwater beneath basins can be ancient — some desert aquifers hold water that fell as rain thousands of years ago.
geology-basin-resources: Sedimentary basins are Earth's treasure chests. Their layered, buried rock traps oil and natural gas in porous reservoirs, hosts coal seams laid down in ancient swamps, and concentrates groundwater that entire regions drink. Salt deposits, evaporites, and even uranium ores accumulate in basin centres. About two-thirds of the world's petroleum is found in just a few giant basins, which is why geologists map basin geometry before drilling a single well.
